When Vision-Language Models Judge Without Seeing: Exposing Informativeness Bias

Xiaohan Zou ††thanks: Work done during internship at Oracle AI. Affiliation: The Pennsylvania State University    Roshan Sridhar Affiliation: Oracle AIxfz5266@psu.edu, {roshan.sridhar, mohammadtaher.safarzadeh, dan.roth}@oracle.com    Mohammadtaher Safarzadeh Affiliation: Oracle AIxfz5266@psu.edu, {roshan.sridhar, mohammadtaher.safarzadeh, dan.roth}@oracle.com    Dan Roth Affiliation: Oracle AIxfz5266@psu.edu, {roshan.sridhar, mohammadtaher.safarzadeh, dan.roth}@oracle.com
Abstract

The reliability of VLM-as-a-Judge is critical for the automatic evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs). Despite recent progress, our analysis reveals that VLM-as-a-Judge often pays limited attention to the image when making decisions. Instead, they often blindly favor the more informative answer, even when they can recognize it conflicts with the image content. We call this problem informativeness bias, which significantly undermines judge reliability. To address it, we propose BIRCH (Balanced Informativeness and CoRrectness with a Truthful AnCHor), a judging paradigm that first corrects inconsistencies with the image content in candidate answers, and then compares the answers against this corrected version. This shifts the judge’s focus from informativeness to image-grounded correctness. Experiments on multiple models and benchmarks show that BIRCH reduces informativeness bias by up to 17%, resulting in performance gains of up to 9.8%. Our work reveals an overlooked but fundamental flaw in current VLM-as-a-Judge systems and highlights the need for more principled designs.

1 Introduction

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of multimodal perception and reasoning tasks OpenAI et al. (2024b); Fu et al. (2024); Yue et al. (2024). Building on this, they are now widely used as automatic judges to evaluate responses and guide reward generation Chen et al. (2024a); Yasunaga et al. (2025). VLM-as-a-Judge is typically applied in pairwise comparison tasks, where two candidate answers to a question about an image are compared to determine which is better. The judgment is then evaluated against human annotations Jing and Du (2025); Yu et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2024), as shown in Figure 2 (A), (B) and (C).

Despite the increasing use of VLM-as-a-Judge, its reliability is still underexplored. In LLM-as-a-Judge, several biases have been reported, such as positional bias, where judges favor certain answer positions Zheng et al. (2023), length bias, where longer responses are preferred Wang et al. (2024a), and authority bias, where fabricated citations reduce judgment accuracy Chen et al. (2024b). These issues raise concerns about fairness and trust in evaluation tasks Gu et al. (2025); Shi et al. (2025); Ye et al. (2025). However, the vision-language setting remains less explored. Existing work on VLM-as-a-Judge mainly focuses on increasing task diversity and difficulty Chen et al. (2024a); Li et al. (2025b); Yasunaga et al. (2025), but often overlooks whether vision-language judgment is being made and evaluated as intended.

To investigate this, we analyzed popular models and found that they pay little attention to images when making judgments. Removing the image from their inputs causes only a minimal drop in performance (Section 4.1). A deeper look reveals a striking behavior: VLM-as-a-Judge is heavily deceived by the answer informativeness, following the definition in Lin et al. (2022); Wu et al. (2025):

They often favor the more informative answer despite clear inconsistencies with the image, even when they can recognize those inconsistencies (Section 4.2). For example, in Figure 2 (A), Answer A is more truthful since it avoids a false claim about the park’s name, but is less informative. Answer B is more informative by providing a name, though it is wrong. This shows that greater informativeness can increase the risk of speculation or error Lin et al. (2022); Wu et al. (2025). However, VLM-as-a-Judge still incorrectly selects Answer B (Figure 2 (C)), despite knowing the image gives no clue about the park’s name (Figure 2 (D)). As a result, VLM-as-a-Judge performs much worse when the more informative answer is wrong than when it happens to be truthful, as shown in Figure 1.

In Section 4.4, we further show that informativeness bias is much stronger than the commonly discussed length bias Zheng et al. (2023); Gu et al. (2025) and remains significant even after controlling for length. This suggests that, although more informative answers tend to be longer, the two biases are not equivalent. Consequently, prior strategies for reducing length bias, such as instructing models to ignore length Zheng et al. (2023) or equalizing response lengths Hu et al. (2025), are insufficient, since informativeness bias cannot be resolved by addressing length effects alone.

In summary, informativeness bias is a key factor that pulls VLM-as-a-Judge away from image content, undermining reliability. As a result, their judging ability lags behind their vision-language understanding, leaving much of that capability underused. To bridge this gap and make VLMs more reliable for evaluation, we propose a novel judging paradigm BIRCH (Balanced Informativeness and CoRrectness with a Truthful AnCHor). The core idea is for the judge to first create a truthful "anchor" that encodes the necessary image content into text. Candidate answers are then compared against this anchor, bringing the judge’s attention back to the image and reducing informativeness bias. To avoid over-prioritizing correctness and unfairly rejecting valid details, the anchor is made as informative as the candidates. We achieve this by asking the judge to revise the candidate answers using the query and image, removing unsupported claims with explanations and fixing inconsistencies. The resulting anchor is both accurate and informative, allowing every detail in the candidates to be verified against it, as described in Section 5.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 8 state-of-the-art judging models, covering both open-source and commercial systems, on two benchmarks. BIRCH consistently achieves better performance than all baselines. We also confirm that BIRCH substantially reduces informativeness bias. As shown in Figure 1, it greatly improves accuracy when the more informative answer is untruthful, demonstrating a stronger focus on image consistency, which drives the performance gains.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We identify informativeness bias, where VLM-as-a-Judge is distracted by the informativeness of answers and pays little attention to image content. This leaves much of its vision-language capability underused for judgment tasks, thereby undermining reliability (Section 4.1, 4.2, and 4.3).

  2. 2.

    We show that informativeness bias is distinct from and cannot be reduced to the commonly discussed length bias (Section 4.4), and thus calls for a solution that goes beyond simply removing length effects.

  3. 3.

    We propose BIRCH, a novel judging paradigm that mitigates informativeness bias and refocuses the judge’s attention on the image, enabling better use of VLM capabilities and improving overall performance (Section 5).

2 Related Work

2.1 LLM/VLM-as-a-Judge Benchmarks

Developing effective LLM/VLM-as-a-Judge systems is essential for evaluating and aligning LLMs and VLMs Ouyang et al. (2022); Grattafiori et al. (2024). Existing benchmarks such as Anthropic Helpful and Harmless Bai et al. (2022), OpenAI Summarization Stiennon et al. (2020), RewardBench Lambert et al. (2025), and JudgeBench Tan et al. (2025) have significantly advanced evaluation in the text modality (LLMs).

To extend this progress to the multimodal domain, MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a) takes the first step in quantifying VLMs’ performance as judges. VL-RewardBench Li et al. (2025b) targets scenarios where even state-of-the-art models struggle. Multimodal RewardBench Yasunaga et al. (2025) incorporates expert knowledge domains and safety-related concerns. Judge Anything Pu et al. (2025) expands this scope to multimodal generation tasks, incorporating both video and audio inputs. MM-RLHF Zhang et al. (2025b) improves size, diversity, annotation granularity, and includes safety-related tasks. However, despite this progress, existing works still lack a critical examination of the reliability of VLM-as-a-Judge behavior.

2.2 Biases in LLM/VLM-as-a-Judge

Recent work has found several cognitive biases that affect how LLMs evaluate Gu et al. (2025). Many studies Zheng et al. (2023); Shi et al. (2025) have discussed biases such as position, verbosity, and self-enhancement. Others Koo et al. (2024) highlight compassion fade, bandwagon effect, and attentional bias. Additional work Chen et al. (2024b); Stureborg et al. (2024) has noted fallacy-oversight, authority, and beauty bias. Ye et al. (2025) propose an automated pipeline to measure diverse biases, while Wei et al. (2025) analyze biases across different prompt templates.

However, this topic remains underexplored in the multimodal domain. While modality bias, where multimodal LLMs over-rely on language Zheng et al. (2025); Li et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025), is well known, its impact on judging behavior remains unclear. The most related work, Li et al. (2025c), shows that over-relying on text-only patterns during training hurts the generalization of multimodal reward models. Our work goes further by linking this issue to over-prioritizing informativeness.

2.3 Debiasing in LLM/VLM-as-a-Judge

To reduce bias in LLM-as-a-Judge, studies have asked judges to follow predefined rules Zeng et al. (2024), provided reference answers to avoid context confusion Zheng et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2025a), swapped response positions to reduce positional bias Wang et al. (2024a), or equalized answer length to reduce length bias Hu et al. (2025). However, these methods are not designed to handle informativeness bias and are therefore ineffective for this issue.

On the multimodal side, Li et al. (2025c) reduces bias from textual spurious correlations by shifting the training distribution toward better multimodal understanding. Our work instead identifies informativeness bias as a cause and addresses it by enforcing attention to image consistency without additional training.

3 Analysis Setup

3.1 Pairwise Comparison in VLM-as-a-Judge

We formalize VLM-as-a-Judge using a pairwise preference comparison paradigm Chen et al. (2024a). Let 𝒟≔{di}i=1N\mathcal{D}\coloneq\{d_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} be a dataset with NN preference examples. Each example di=(Qi,Ii,yic,yir)d_{i}=(Q_{i},I_{i},y^{c}_{i},y^{r}_{i}) contains a question about an image, the image itself, and two responses labeled by human preference. Here, QiQ_{i} is the textual query, IiI_{i} is the associated image, yicy^{c}_{i} is the preferred response, and yiry^{r}_{i} is the less preferred one. For simplicity, we drop the subscript ii when the context is clear.

The judge model f⁡(Q,I,yc,yr)f(Q,I,y^{c},y^{r}) takes a sample as input and decides which answer better addresses the question. Its performance is measured by accuracy against human preferences:

Acc=𝔼(Q,I,yc,yr)∼𝒟​[𝕀⁡(f⁡(Q,I,yc,yr)=yc)].\text{Acc}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(Q,I,y^{c},y^{r})\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\mathbb{I}\big(f(Q,I,y^{c},y^{r})=y^{c}\big)\Big].

3.2 Quantifying Image Reliance

VLMs are known to underuse visual content and over-rely on text Li et al. (2024); Fu et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025); Leng et al. (2024). We ask whether they show a similar tendency when used as judges and measure how much they rely on visual input. Specifically, we define the Image Reliance Score (IRS) as the accuracy gap of judge model ff when evaluated with and without the image II as input:

IRS=𝔼(Q,I,yc,yr)∼𝒟​[𝕀⁡(f⁡(Q,I,yc,yr)=yc)]−𝔼(Q,yc,yr)∼𝒟​[𝕀⁡(f⁡(Q,yc,yr)=yc)].\begin{split}\text{IRS}=\mathbb{E}_{(Q,I,y^{c},y^{r})\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\mathbb{I}\big(f(Q,I,y^{c},y^{r})=y^{c}\big)\Big]\\ -\mathbb{E}_{(Q,y^{c},y^{r})\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\mathbb{I}\big(f(Q,y^{c},y^{r})=y^{c}\big)\Big].\end{split}

A VLM judge that depends more on image content will have a higher IRS, since its accuracy improves more when the image is included.

3.3 Judging Informativeness

General-purpose alignment aims to produce responses that balance correctness and informativeness Zheng et al. (2023). This is reflected in common judging prompts, which often include rubrics such as: "Your evaluation should consider factors such as accuracy, helpfulness, relevance, depth, and level of detail" Zheng et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2024a), encouraging responses to go beyond a minimal correct answer and provide additional context Lin et al. (2022). Here, accuracy corresponds to correctness, which requires using the image to detect errors or inconsistencies, while helpfulness, relevance, depth, and level of detail correspond to informativeness, which can be judged from the answers alone. We focus on how informativeness affects VLM-as-a-Judge behavior, so we separate it from the other judging criteria.

Based on this, we define the rubrics for informativeness as helpfulness, relevance, depth, and level of detail, with accuracy removed from the original set. We then ask GPT-4o to decide which answer, ycy^{c} or yry^{r}, is more informative using these rubrics. The full prompt is in Appendix A. Only the textual query QQ and the two candidate answers (yc,yr)(y^{c},y^{r}) are given, while the image II is withheld, since informativeness does not depend on it. GPT-4o is explicitly instructed to judge only on informativeness, without considering correctness or consistency with the image. The output is yiy^{i}, the more informative answer, where yiy^{i} is either ycy^{c} or yry^{r}. See Appendix C.1 for an evaluation of the reliability of GPT-4o in measuring informativeness

3.4 Measuring Informativeness Bias

Several studies have shown that prioritizing informativeness can come at the cost of correctness Zhou et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2025). We define Informativeness Bias (IB) as the degree to which a judge favors informativeness over correctness.

We split the preference dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} into two subsets. The informativeness-driven subset 𝒟IDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}} contains cases where the human-preferred answer ycy^{c} is more informative than yry^{r} (i.e., yc=yiy^{c}=y^{i}), meaning informativeness is a valid factor. The correctness-driven subset 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} includes cases where the preferred answer ycy^{c} is less informative (i.e., yr=yiy^{r}=y^{i}), meaning correctness is the main factor and informativeness is misleading. We compute IB as:

IB=𝔼d∼𝒟IDS[𝕀(f(d)=yc)](AccIDS)−𝔼d∼𝒟CDS​[𝕀⁡(f⁡(d)=yc)](AccCDS).\begin{split}\text{IB}&=\mathbb{E}_{d\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}}}\Big[\mathbb{I}\big(f(d)=y^{c}\big)\Big]\quad(\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}})\\ &-\mathbb{E}_{d\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}}}\Big[\mathbb{I}\big(f(d)=y^{c}\big)\Big]\quad(\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}}).\end{split}

In other words, we treat human annotators as unbiased, and obviously IB=0\text{IB}=0 for humans since their AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} and AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} are both 100%. For an unbiased judge, IB should also be close to zero, meaning it performs equally well whether or not informativeness is misleading. A positive IB indicates the judge performs better on 𝒟IDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}}, showing a preference for informativeness. An ideal judge should achieve high AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} and AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} for strong overall performance, while keeping IB low to balance informativeness and correctness.

3.5 Measuring Length Bias

Prior studies show that LLM-as-a-Judge often favors longer responses, known as length bias Zheng et al. (2023); Ye et al. (2025). Since informativeness is often tied to length, with more informative answers usually being longer, we also measure Length Bias (LB) for comparison to investigate how the two biases relate.

Following the definition of informativeness bias, we split the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} into two subsets, one where the longer answer is preferred and one where the shorter answer is preferred. We then calculate LB as the difference in a judge’s accuracy between them: LB=Accyc​ is longer−Accyc​ is shorter\text{LB}=\text{Acc}_{y^{c}\text{ is longer}}-\text{Acc}_{y^{c}\text{ is shorter}}. The magnitude |LB||\text{LB}| shows how strongly the judge is influenced by length, while the sign shows whether it favors longer or shorter responses.

4 Exposing Informativeness Bias

4.1 Judges Are Nearly Blind to Images

Table 1 shows that the Image Reliance Score (IRS) is minimal across all models and benchmarks, meaning image content provides only negligible gains (less than 3% on MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a) and under 5% on VL-RewardBench Li et al. (2025b)). We further divide MLLM-as-a-Judge into different source domains and show in Figure 11 that adding the image yields only slight accuracy improvements across all domains, and in some cases even reduces performance. This suggests that VLM-as-a-Judge often ignores the image when evaluating answers to VQA questions, raising concerns about their reliability and highlighting the need for deeper investigation of this issue.

4.2 Judges Are Deceived by Informativeness

Judges over-prioritize informativeness. As shown in Figure 3, we find significant informativeness bias (IB): over 30% for Gemini-2.5-Flash and over 50% for other models. We also report IB variance by downsampling 𝒟IDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}} and 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} at different ratios (see Appendix C.3), showing reasonably low variance. The high IB is also clear in Figure 9, where AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} is always much higher than AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}}. These indicate that VLM judges perform far worse when informativeness is misleading, revealing their strong tendency to overvalue informativeness.

Judge performance heavily depends on how often informativeness is misleading. We downsample to control the ratio of the correctness-driven subset 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} and examine how performance changes with it. A higher ratio means informativeness is misleading more often. As shown in Figure 4, judge accuracies decrease as the proportion of 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} grows. Since the proportion of 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} is low in the original benchmark (32%), judges can appear strong overall (>65%) even with poor AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} (Figure 9). But with a balanced ratio (50%), which better reflects their real performance, overall accuracy drops to around 55%, only slightly above random guessing. This reveals a serious and previously overlooked unreliability in VLM-as-a-Judge.

Judges are misled by informativeness, even when they know the correct answer. We show that poor AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} is not due to a lack of vision-language ability in the judge. As illustrated in Figure 2 (D) and additional examples in Appendix D, when directly prompted to answer the question QQ, the judge often produces a correct response that aligns with the human-chosen answer and points out inconsistencies or errors in the rejected one. Yet, when acting as a judge, it still selects the human-rejected answer as the better choice, contradicting its own response. A common pattern is that the chosen answer appears more informative, offering detailed explanations or direct answers, but without considering correctness.

These findings show that judges can understand questions and spot conflicts between answers and the image. However, they are deceived by informativeness, giving it far more weight than correctness.

4.3 Informativeness Bias Pulls Judge’s Attention Away from the Image

From Section 4.1 and 4.2, we hypothesize that informativeness bias (IB) distracts the judge’s attention from the image, leading to a low image reliance score (IRS). We now verify this connection.

Image reliance is higher on correctness-driven cases 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}}. As shown in Figure 5, IRS is consistently higher on correctness-driven cases 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} than on informativeness-driven cases 𝒟IDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}} across all models and benchmarks, indicating that judges rely more on images when correctness drives the decision. This supports our hypothesis: when informativeness is misleading, correctness becomes crucial, and as correctness cannot be verified without the image, visual input is far more valuable.

Informativeness bias worsens when the judge lacks image input. We test how removing the image from the judge’s input affects IB. As shown in Figure 6, judges without images consistently show stronger IB than those with images, with gaps of up to 18.6%. This also supports our claim: without the image, the judge cannot verify correctness and is forced to rely only on informativeness.

4.4 Informativeness Bias Is Distinct from Length Bias

Figure 3 compares informativeness bias (IB) with length bias (LB). LB is consistently much weaker, trailing IB by about 30% or more across all models and benchmarks. Figure 8 further breaks this down and shows IB is higher than LB in nearly all domains. This suggests that IB is not merely a proxy for LB; rather, it might be a more substantial issue.

To investigate further, we remove the effect of LB by creating a version of the MLLM-as-a-Judge benchmark where the length difference between candidate answers is below a small threshold (see Appendix C.5). Table 2 shows IB after this length equalization. While IB decreases, it remains substantial (26%-45.5%). This suggests that, although IB and LB are correlated, IB cannot be resolved by addressing LB alone, as a substantial portion of IB remains after controlling for length. The correlation is expected, since more informative answers are often longer, making a preference for informativeness appear as a preference for length. However, mitigating IB requires directly addressing informativeness bias rather than focusing only on length effects Zheng et al. (2023); Hu et al. (2025).

5 Method

Based on Section 4, VLM-as-a-Judge can answer questions correctly but gets distracted by informativeness and fails to focus on the image. Therefore, we explore whether using its own answer as a reference can refocus attention on image consistency. Unlike prior work that improves LLM-as-a-Judge by providing ground-truth references Zheng et al. (2023); Hagos et al. (2024); Zhou et al. (2025), we instead use a self-generated reference.

5.1 Reducing Informativeness Bias

Figure 12 illustrates the Standard Ref pipeline. The model first answers the question directly, encoding key image details relevant to the question into a textual reference. It then judges by comparing the two candidate answers to this reference. This naturally shifts the focus from informativeness alone to consistency with the image, since the reference already includes image details.

Figure 12 (A) shows a successful case: with its own answer as reference, the judge correctly detects that Answer B gives a park name not visible in the image and selects Answer A instead. Table 4 confirms that this greatly reduces informativeness bias (IB) and improves AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}}, boosting performance when correctness should drive the decision.

However, this approach can also cause judges to over-prioritize correctness and unfairly reject valid details in candidates simply because they are missing from the reference. In Figure 12 (B), Answer A is rejected just for mentioning the correct position of a sign omitted in the reference. Table 4 shows a clear drop in AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}}, meaning the judge performs worse when informativeness should guide the decision. This matches prior findings Wu et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2023) that greater emphasis on correctness often leads to over-caution about extra information. As a result, while this method improves AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} and lowers IB, it still reduces overall accuracy compared to the base pipeline.

5.2 Our Method: BIRCH

We propose BIRCH, which balances informativeness and correctness using an "anchor" that is both truthful and as informative as the candidates. As shown in Figure 7, the judge first modifies each candidate answer by correcting inconsistencies with the image or removing unsupported claims with explanations. The corrected answers are then merged into a single anchor. This ensures the generated anchor encodes the truthful version of all relevant image details included in the candidates. As a result, when candidates are compared to the anchor, every detail can be verified against it, preserving informativeness while enforcing correctness.

6 Experiments

6.1 Evaluation Settings

We evaluate our approach on MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a) and VL-RewardBench Li et al. (2025b) benchmarks. We use a pairwise comparison setup Chen et al. (2024a); Li et al. (2025b) to measure agreement between model and human judgments. We manually corrected human labeling errors that reduced benchmark reliability and evaluated on the revised data (see Appendix B).

Our experiments include open-source models such as Phi-4-multimodal Abdin et al. (2024), LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-8B Li et al. (2025a), LLaVA-1.5-13B, LLaVA-1.6-34B Liu et al. (2024), and Llama-3.2-Vision-90B Grattafiori et al. (2024), as well as commercial models like GPT-4o OpenAI et al. (2024b), Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Gemini-2.5-Pro Comanici et al. (2025).

6.2 Evaluation of BIRCH

Main Results. As shown in Table 3, BIRCH achieves the best performance across all tested models and benchmarks, with improvements over Base (a standard judge pipeline following Chen et al. (2024a) with no extra input) ranging from 2.73% to 9.84%. Improvements are larger on stronger models like GPT-4o, Gemini, and Llama-3.2. Although these models are affected by informativeness bias, their stronger vision ability helps them detect and correct errors in candidate answers and generate more reliable anchors. Gains are smaller for weaker models such as LLaVA-1.5/1.6, which lack strong vision understanding, and for Phi-4-Multimodal, which shows less informativeness bias to begin with (see Appendix C.6), leaving less room for improvement.

Ablation Studies. BIRCH introduces an anchor generation module that corrects and merges candidate answers to assist the judge. To evaluate this design, Table 3 compares it with two alternatives: (1) Image Caption, which generates an image caption and uses it with the query, image, and candidate answers for judging, as illustrated in Figure 13, and (2) Standard Ref, which produces a reference answer without using the candidates and then compares the candidates against it, as described in Section 5.1. BIRCH outperforms all baselines. Image Caption and Standard Ref sometimes slightly outperform Base, but in some cases they perform worse than Base.

6.3 Why BIRCH Works Well?

Quantitative Results. We analyze changes across multiple metrics with and without BIRCH in Table 2 and 8. BIRCH shows a much lower IB than both Base and Standard Ref across all models. For GPT-4o, BIRCH boosts AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} by 19% over Base, much higher than the gain from Standard Ref, and also raises AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} by 4.8% at the same time, resulting in a 9.3% overall accuracy gain. In contrast, Standard Ref causes a 4.6% drop in AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}}, which finally lowers overall accuracy. These results show that BIRCH maintains a good balance without over-prioritizing or over-penalizing informativeness. Moreover, BIRCH also clearly reduces length bias (LB), consistent with our finding that IB and LB are not independent and that mitigating IB also alleviates LB.

Case study. We provide qualitative examples in Figure 7, 12, 13 and Appendix D to illustrate how BIRCH balances informativeness and correctness, and why Standard Ref and Image Caption fail. Base is easily misled by a more informative but incorrect answer, even when it clearly conflicts with the judge’s own response. BIRCH creates an anchor by correcting or removing inconsistencies while preserving valid details. This allows the judge to verify every detail in the candidates and make correct judgments. In contrast, Standard Ref and Image Caption generate references without using the candidate answers and often miss details mentioned in them. As a result, Standard Ref makes the judge overly cautious and reject correct details that are not in the reference, while Image Caption accepts unsupported details when they cannot be verified against the caption. BIRCH reduces both incorrect rejection and acceptance and achieves a better balance.

6.4 Anchor Quality

The effectiveness of BIRCH depends on the quality of the generated anchors. These anchors should contain fewer factual errors than the original candidate answers to help the judge verify image details. To evaluate this, we use GPT-5 to score the correctness of the anchors and the two original candidate answers for Gemini-2.5-Flash and LLaVA-1.5-13B. As shown in Table 5, the anchors achieve higher average scores than both original answers, indicating that VLMs can correct many image inconsistencies and produce more accurate anchors.

6.5 Inference Effencify

Although anchor generation in BIRCH involves two steps, answer correction and merging, they are implemented in a single pass, as shown in Table 20. Therefore, BIRCH requires only one additional pass compared to the plain judge pipeline Base.

We further illustrate this by reporting the average inference time per data point in seconds for LLaVA-One-Vision-1.5-8B on a single A100 GPU for BIRCH and Base in Table 6. The inference time of BIRCH is about twice that of Base, which is expected since it performs one extra pass. This overhead is comparable to or lower than many LLM-as-a-judge methods Tang et al. (2024); Khan et al. (2024) that require multiple extra calls.

7 Conclusion

We reveal and address a fundamental flaw in current VLM-as-a-Judge systems, namely informativeness bias, the tendency to blindly favor more informative answers while giving little attention to the image. To improve reliability, we propose BIRCH, which compares candidate answers against a self-generated anchor that corrects or verifies all image details mentioned. This shifts the judge’s focus back to image content, ensuring every detail is properly verified and thus balancing informativeness with correctness. BIRCH substantially reduces informativeness bias and delivers consistent gains across multiple VLMs and benchmarks.

8 Limitations

Our work analyzes the issues that undermine the reliability of VLM-as-a-Judge and proposes BIRCH to reduce informativeness bias and refocus on image content for more truthful judgments. BIRCH is simple to implement and requires no extra training.

However, informativeness bias still remains after applying BIRCH (Table 3), which shows that it does not fully resolve the problem. Future work could address the following issues. BIRCH builds an anchor by correcting candidate answers to encode key image details and guide the judge toward correctness. However, the model can still be influenced by informativeness during this process and fail to remove or fix incorrect claims, which reduces the quality of the anchor. Besides, even when BIRCH generates a reliable and accurate anchor, the judge may still favor a more informative but incorrect answer (Appendix D.3).

In addition, BIRCH is designed to boost performance by reducing informativeness bias. However, for models like Phi-4-Multimodal, where the bias is already small (Section C.6), the gains are limited (Table 3). Future work should explore ways to further strengthen judging ability in such models.

9 Ethical Considerations

In this paper, we introduce BIRCH, a new judging framework designed to make VLM-as-a-Judge more reliable and better aligned with human preferences. However, human annotators themselves are subject to bias, which in turn makes aligning VLM-as-a-Judge with their preferences also biased. We leave mitigating such biases in both benchmarks and VLM-as-a-Judge to future work.

Appendix B Benchmark Details

B.1 Introduction

MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a)

is the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal LLMs as judges. It contains 4,414 image-instruction pairs from 14 datasets covering tasks such as image captioning, math reasoning, text reading, and infographic understanding. Candidate answers are generated using six MLLMs: GPT-4V OpenAI et al. (2024a), Gemini-Pro-Vision Team et al. (2025), LLaVA-1.5-13b, LLaVA-1.6-34b Liu et al. (2024), CogVLM Wang et al. (2024c), and Qwen-VL-Max Wang et al. (2024b). The benchmark provides three settings: (1) scoring evaluation, where each answer is rated from 1 to 5, (2) pairwise comparison, where two answers are compared to select the better one, and (3) batch ranking, where answers are ordered by quality. In our work, we use only the pairwise comparison setting, which includes 7,756 samples.

VL-RewardBench Li et al. (2025b)

focuses on the pairwise comparison setting, with 1,247 samples from 7 datasets. It includes hallucination-oriented queries in addition to general instruction-following and reasoning tasks, and provides error-type labels. To ensure the samples are challenging enough to expose model weaknesses, it only keeps cases where multiple smaller models (such as LLaVA-1.5/1.6-7B Liu et al. (2024) and Qwen2-VL-7B Wang et al. (2024b)) make errors.

B.2 Preprocessing

We found that human annotators made many errors when labeling the better candidate answer in the benchmarks we used. Figures 14, 15, 16 and 17 show examples of such errors. These mistakes undermine the reliability of evaluating VLM-as-a-Judge. To address this, we manually reviewed the data samples and corrected the identified errors before evaluation.

Appendix C More Experiment Details

C.1 Reliability of Informativeness Measuring

As described in Section 3.3, we use GPT-4o to measure informativeness, and our analysis depends on its reliability. To validate this, we randomly sample 100 examples from each benchmark, MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a) and VL-RewardBench Li et al. (2025b), and ask human annotators to decide which candidate is more informative based on text alone, using the same rubric as GPT-4o (Figure 18). We then measure agreement between human and GPT-4o using match rate, which is the percentage of matching cases in [0, 1], and Cohen’s kappa Cohen (1960) in [-1, 1], where higher values indicate better agreement.

Table 7 shows that the match rate exceeds 0.9 and Cohen’s kappa exceeds 0.8, indicating strong agreement between GPT-4o and human judgments and confirming its reliability for comparing informativeness.

C.2 Image Reliance Across Domains

Figure 11 shows a per-domain comparison of GPT-4o OpenAI et al. (2024a), Llama-3.2-Vision-90B Grattafiori et al. (2024), and Gemini-2.5-Flash Comanici et al. (2025), with and without image input on the MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a) benchmark. Most domains lie close to the diagonal, showing that images add little benefit and sometimes even reduce performance.

C.3 Downsampling Details for Section 4.2

We compute informativeness bias (IB) and length bias (LB) by subtracting accuracy on different subsets (Section 3.4 and 3.5). Since this can be affected by randomness, variance, and differences in sample selection or subset size, we mitigate it by downsampling each subset at different ratios multiple times. We report the mean across all samples, and show variance bars in Figures 3 and 10.

Specifically, for IB the two subsets are 𝒟IDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}} and 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}}, and for LB they are 𝒟yc​ is longer\mathcal{D}_{y^{c}\text{ is longer}} and 𝒟yc​ is shorter\mathcal{D}_{y^{c}\text{ is shorter}}. We downsample each at 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% (full set), with 10 samples per ratio. This results in 4×4×10=1604\times 4\times 10=160 downsamplings for each IB or LB computation.

The variance from this process is reasonably low (see Figures 3 and 10), confirming the validity of our results.

C.4 Informativeness Bias Across Domains

Figure 8 compares informativeness bias (IB) and length bias (LB) across domains in MLLM-as-a-Judge, showing that IB is higher than LB in almost all cases. Figure 9 presents AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} and AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}}, the accuracies for the informativeness-driven and correctness-driven subsets. A large gap appears, with AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} much higher. Together, these results indicate that IB is far more significant than LB.

C.5 Ablation of Length Bias

Inspired by Ye et al. (2025); Hu et al. (2025), we separate length bias from informativeness bias by equalizing the lengths (measured in words) of the two answers. Specifically, before computing informativeness bias, we extend the shorter answer by asking GPT-4o to lengthen its existing content until it matches the longer one. We strictly instruct GPT-4o not to add any new information beyond the original answer, and to increase length only by repeating existing content or adding verbosity.

After this, we recheck the dataset and keep only samples where the length difference between the two answers is within a small threshold (5 words). This process removes the effect of length bias, since both answers are made nearly equal in length.

C.6 Lower Informativeness Bias for Phi-4-Multimodal

Figure 10 compares informativeness bias (IB) and length bias (LB) for Phi-4-Multimodal Abdin et al. (2024). To reduce randomness and variance, we report mean and variance computed by downsampling 𝒟IDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{IDS}} and 𝒟CDS\mathcal{D}_{\text{CDS}} at different ratios multiple times, as described in Appendix C.3. Phi-4-Multimodal shows IB below 30% on both benchmarks, significantly lower than other models (see Figure 3, where IB is around 60%).

This explains why BIRCH yields smaller improvements on Phi-4-Multimodal, as it is designed to reduce IB, and Phi-4-Multimodal already has low IB. As shown in Table 8, BIRCH improves AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} by only 5.3% and reduces IB by 2.0% for Phi-4-Multimodal, much lower than the gains observed on other models.

C.7 Why BIRCH Works Well

Table 8 extends Table 4 and reports changes across multiple metrics for other models before and after applying BIRCH on the MLLM-as-a-Judge Chen et al. (2024a) benchmark.

BIRCH consistently reduces informativeness bias (IB) by substantially improving AccCDS\text{Acc}_{\text{CDS}} while keeping AccIDS\text{Acc}_{\text{IDS}} strong across all models, leading to higher overall performance. Although designed to mitigate IB, BIRCH also greatly reduces length bias (LB), further supporting our finding that IB and LB are intertwined and that addressing IB also reduces LB.

Appendix D More Case Studies

D.1 Judges Misled by Informativeness, Mitigated by a Reference Answer

Figures 22, 23 (MLLM-as-a-Judge), and 24 (VL-RewardBench) provide additional qualitative examples showing how VLM-as-a-Judge is misled by a more informative but wrong answer, even when it clearly conflicts with the judge’s own response. However, when the judge uses its own answer as a reference, it can easily detect inconsistencies with the image and select the correct choice.

D.2 Why BIRCH outperforms Standard Ref?

Figures 25, 26, 27 (MLLM-as-a-Judge), and 28 (VL-RewardBench) present qualitative examples showing why Standard Ref, which generates a reference without considering the candidate answers, performs poorly in some cases, and why our BIRCH works better.

In Standard Ref, many details from the candidate answers may be missing in the reference. As a result, the judge often treats these extra but unverifiable details as wrong, even if they are actually correct. This leads to over-caution, an excessive focus on correctness, and weaker performance on informativeness-driven cases.

In contrast, BIRCH ensures that every detail in the candidates is reflected in the reference, either corrected, removed with explanation, or preserved if valid. This way, the judge can always verify each detail against the reference, maintaining attention to correctness with image content while also preserving informativeness.

D.3 Failure Case Analysis

We analyze failure cases where informativeness is misleading and explain why informativeness bias can persist even after applying BIRCH.

In Figure 29, the correct answer is 5,200 million. Answer A is correct, while Answer B incorrectly states 5.2 million. BIRCH fails to correct this inconsistency and includes it in the anchor. This may be due to limited visual or reasoning ability of the VLM, or because the model is still influenced by informativeness during anchor generation.

In Figure 30, Answer 1 correctly states that the balloon is filled with a light gas. Answer 2 is more informative but does not specify what the balloon is filled with, so Answer 1 is better. In this case, the anchor is reliable, but BIRCH is still misled by the more informative Answer 2. This shows that anchors alone are not sufficient to eliminate informativeness bias, and we leave this limitation to future work.
